title: Coins That Corrected the Chronicle
subtitle: When Silent Coins Spoke Louder Than a Royal Chronicle
era: Modern numismatic reassessment, 1977-1986, of coinage from c. 1467 onward
region: Tripura royal collections, Ujjayanta Palace museum and Bengal numismatic scholarship
moral: Evidence can honor tradition while correcting it.

sources.citation: Manikya dynasty coin corpus, 774 gold, silver and copper coins in Ujjayanta Palace museum
sources.note: The fullest non-textual primary record of the dynasty.

sources.citation: N.N. Bhattacharyya, Coinage of the Tripura Rajas (1986)
sources.note: Definitive numismatic reassessment of early Manikya chronology.

sources.citation: D.C. Sircar, Epigraphia Indica vol. 41 (1975-76) and Studies in the History of India (1979)
sources.note: Epigraphic framework for correcting the sequence.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle close-up of a hand holding an ancient Tripura coin against the dim outline of Ujjayanta Palace

dialogue.text: In Ujjayanta’s quiet vaults, N.N. Bhattacharyya let 774 small coins challenge a royal chronicle and turn the Manikya past on its head.

panels.shot: slow push-in through museum hall into a table scattered with trays of coins

dialogue.text: Tripura’s kings had a poem, the Rajmala, to sing their line. But on this table lay their other testimony: 774 coins, each a tiny, stubborn document in metal.

panels.shot: top-down macro shot on open palm holding three distinct Manikya coins

dialogue.text: For centuries, most historians trusted the Rajmala’s order: Dharma Manikya, then Ratna Manikya, and a Manikya title gifted by a Bengal sultan. The coins whispered another sequence.

panels.shot: side profile close-up of Bhattacharyya peering through a magnifying glass

dialogue.text: A numismatist lives by minute things: a date squeezed into a margin, a title slightly altered, an image borrowed, a mint mark moved. Here, every dot of Nagari and Persian mattered.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bhattacharyya and a young assistant at a desk, books and coins open

dialogue.speaker: n_n_bhattacharyya
dialogue.text: We will let sequence, not sentiment, decide their place.

panels.shot: split-panel feel: left shows palm-leaf Rajmala, right shows coin close-up

dialogue.text: The Rajmala told a flowing story, shaped by court poets and the pride of a house. The coins were blunt records of who ruled, what they claimed, and how they minted power.

panels.shot: macro shot of a Ratna Manikya coin showing mixed scripts and design

dialogue.text: Ratna Manikya’s coins wore two faces: layouts and calligraphy echoing the Bengal sultans, yet legends invoking Hindu deities and the old Manikya name. Metal mirrored a frontier king’s tightrope.

panels.shot: diagrammatic-style wide shot of coins arranged in chronological rows on felt

dialogue.text: When Bhattacharyya laid the coins in order of style, fabric and weight, a pattern emerged. Legends shifted, titles lengthened, religious formulas changed step by step. Ratna did not stand at the beginning.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of Bhattacharyya writing notes beside Sircar’s book

dialogue.text: D.C. Sircar’s inscriptions gave dates and names carved in stone. When these were matched with the coins, the Rajmala’s early ladder tilted. Dharma’s coins came first; Ratna’s followed.

panels.shot: medium shot of Bhattacharyya presenting his argument to unseen scholarly audience

dialogue.speaker: n_n_bhattacharyya
dialogue.text: The coin series compels us: Ratna Manikya succeeds, not precedes, Dharma.

panels.shot: close-up of another coin bearing the Manikya title predating Sultanate-style features

dialogue.text: Another surprise lay in the title itself. Coins with the Manikya name appeared before Ratna’s Sultanate-style issues. The title did not begin as a sultan’s gift, but as a Tripura inheritance.

panels.shot: wide shot comparing a Bengal Sultanate coin and a Ratna Manikya coin side by side

dialogue.text: Ratna’s borrowing of Bengal forms told another story: of influence and negotiation, not of a name bestowed from above. Devotional legends on his coins asserted a parallel, not a subordinate, authority.

panels.shot: macro shot of Amar Manikya’s coin noted as from Sylhet, with riverine motifs

dialogue.text: Later, coins like Amar Manikya’s Sylhet issue quietly recorded political reach. Long after campaigns faded from memory, the mint’s mark on metal still claimed where Tripura’s power had once stood.

panels.shot: intimate close-up of Bhattacharyya’s hand writing the title of his book

dialogue.text: By 1986, his study of these coins took shape as a book: a new backbone for Tripura’s early history, built on weights, legends and calligraphy rather than only on court verse.

panels.shot: wide shot of Ujjayanta Palace museum gallery with coins displayed in lit cases

dialogue.text: Decades later, Ujjayanta reopened as a state museum. The Manikya coins, once scattered in royal hoards, now shone in ordered cases, inviting new eyes, new questions, new cross-checks.

panels.shot: montage-like wide shot of digital screens showing British Museum and ANS catalog entries

dialogue.text: As British and American collections began cataloguing Manikya pieces, Tripura’s coins stepped onto a wider stage. Each new specimen could confirm, refine or challenge the sequence he proposed.

panels.shot: soft low-angle shot of Bhattacharyya seated quietly in the gallery, observing visitors

dialogue.speaker: n_n_bhattacharyya
dialogue.text: Let them read the coins, and then return to the poem.

panels.shot: symbolic close-up of a coin and a palm-leaf manuscript lying side by side

dialogue.text: Bhattacharyya did not erase the Rajmala; he re-grounded it. With Sircar’s inscriptions and the coins as anchors, the early Manikya story could be retold without tearing from tradition.

panels.shot: final contemplative macro shot of a worn coin edge catching light in darkness

dialogue.text: In the end, his work reminds us that history is a dialogue between song and evidence, and that sometimes a tiny, tarnished coin can gently correct a king’s own chronicle.
